guides.title: Finding Direction
guides.summary: Direction from the sun, stars and a watch.

sections.heading: Use the Compass
sections.body: The app's Compass works offline and shows true north using the World Magnetic Model. Note a landmark on your bearing before moving.

sections.heading: Sun
sections.body: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west everywhere. At local noon it is due south in the Northern Hemisphere (due north in the Southern). A shadow stick: mark a shadow tip, wait 15+ min, mark again — the line between marks runs roughly west-to-east.

sections.heading: Stars (Northern Hemisphere)
sections.body: Find the Big Dipper; the two stars at the end of its 'cup' point to Polaris, the North Star, which sits over true north. (Diagram: AstroOgier, CC0 / public domain.)

sections.heading: Stars (Southern Hemisphere)
sections.body: Find the Southern Cross; extend its long axis ~4.5x its length to an empty point — straight down from there is roughly south.

sections.heading: Find north by shadow-stick
sections.body: Works in both hemispheres, any sunny day. Push a straight stick upright into flat ground. Mark the TIP of its shadow with a stone — call this point WEST. Wait 15-20 minutes and mark the new shadow tip — this is EAST. The line joining the two marks runs roughly WEST-EAST (first mark west, second east); a line at right angles to it points NORTH-SOUTH. Stand with west on your left and east on your right and you are facing north.

sections.heading: Analog-watch method
sections.body: With an analog watch set to true local time (no daylight-saving offset): in the NORTHERN hemisphere, point the HOUR hand at the sun; the point halfway between the hour hand and the 12 marks SOUTH. In the SOUTHERN hemisphere, point the 12 at the sun instead; halfway between 12 and the hour hand marks NORTH. No watch? Draw a clock face in the dirt with the hands in the current time and use the same rule.

sections.heading: Reading the Landscape: Vegetation, Snow, and Wind Sign
sections.body:
Every scout manual repeats the same tidy rule: moss grows on the north side of trees. Every scout manual is repeating a half-truth that gets people turned around. Moss needs moisture and shade to establish, and in a Northern Hemisphere temperate forest the north side of a trunk does often receive less direct sun and so does often stay damper — but 'often' is not 'always,' and a single mossy trunk beside a stream, under a canopy gap, or on the shaded downhill side of a slope will happily grow moss facing whichever way keeps it wet, compass be damned. Treat mossy bark as, at best, one weak vote among several, never a verdict on its own.

The clue that actually holds up under scrutiny is asymmetric crown growth on an isolated tree standing in the open — a lone oak in a field, not one crowded by neighbors. In the Northern Hemisphere such a tree spends its life reaching toward the sun's stronger, more direct light from the south, and its branches grow measurably longer and its foliage measurably denser on that equator-facing side, giving the whole crown a lopsided lean toward the south. It's a real effect, driven by phototropism, and it's most reliable on solitary trees with no neighbor shading them from one side.

In snow country the ground itself keeps a written record of the wind. Persistent prevailing winds carve snow into hard, wave-like ridges called sastrugi, aligned parallel to the wind's long-term direction and often scoured sharp on the windward face, softer and drifted on the lee. Roald Amundsen's polar parties, and generations of Inuit travelers before them, read sastrugi fields the way sailors read swells — not as a direct compass bearing, but as a durable, large-scale arrow that keeps pointing the same way for days or weeks after any single storm has passed, which matters precisely because it survives when the sky is a flat, featureless white that swallows both sun and stars. Cross-check it against any other clue you have — a known prevailing wind for the region, a chart's wind rose, or a brief compass or sun sighting whenever the weather breaks — because sastrugi only tells you the wind's direction, not true north, and if you don't independently know which way that wind usually blows, the ridges alone are just texture.

sections.heading: Overcast Skies: Reading Polarized Light and the Brightest Patch
sections.body:
A solid grey overcast feels like it erases the sun entirely, but it rarely does so completely. Clouds thin unevenly, and the patch of sky directly around the sun's position is almost always noticeably brighter, sometimes with a faint yellow-white glow, even when the disc itself is fully hidden. Shade your eyes from the brightest general area with a raised hand rather than staring toward it — a diffused solar disc behind thin cloud can still damage your retina — and you can usually narrow the sun's bearing to within 20-30°, enough to combine with a shadow-stick reading the moment a gap opens.

There's a subtler and older trick for the same problem. Sunlight scattered by the atmosphere is polarized in a pattern that forms bands centered on the sun and its opposite point in the sky, strongest roughly 90° away from the sun's true position. Rotate a pair of polarized sunglasses, or any polarizing camera filter, while looking at a patch of blue sky or even bright thin overcast, and you'll see it darken and lighten as you turn the lens — the axis along which it darkens most traces a great circle running through the sun. Medieval Icelandic sagas describe Norse sailors using a birefringent crystal — a 'sunstone,' most likely calcite (Iceland spar) or cordierite — for exactly this purpose on cloudy northern seas, splitting incoming light into two polarized rays and rotating the crystal until their brightness matched, which happens along that same sun-aligned axis. A genuine 16th-century calcite crystal recovered from an English shipwreck near Alderney was later analyzed by physicists and shown to perform the trick with workable accuracy. You don't need a birefringent crystal today — cheap polarized sunglass lenses do the identical physics — but treat the result as a rough bearing to refine with other methods, not a precision tool.

sections.heading: The Moon as a Backup Compass
sections.body:
On a clear night with a bright moon overhead but no stars you recognize, the moon itself carries directional information — you just have to know its phase to read it correctly, because its position in the sky depends on how far it has traveled around its orbit from the sun, not on any fixed compass point.

The cleanest reading comes from a half-moon. At first quarter — the phase where the moon is half-lit and climbing the evening sky — it sits 90° east of the sun along the ecliptic, which means it crosses your local meridian, standing due south for a Northern Hemisphere observer (due north if you're south of the equator), right around sunset. See a half-moon riding high at dusk, and you already have a strong due-south reference with no arithmetic required. At last quarter — the mirror phase, rising around midnight — the same due-south (or due-north) transit happens around sunrise instead.

A full moon is simpler still but less immediately useful: it sits opposite the sun in the sky, so it rises in the east right as the sun sets in the west, and sets in the west right as the sun rises in the east — a full moon low on the horizon at nightfall is rising almost due east, the same point the sun cleared that morning, give or take the seasonal swing that shifts sunrise itself away from true east.

For a slim crescent, sailors and scouts have long used the horns-of-the-moon trick: draw an imaginary straight line connecting the two pointed cusps of the crescent and extend it down to the horizon — the point where it lands is a rough approximation of south in the Northern Hemisphere. Treat it as exactly that: rough. The line's accuracy swings by tens of degrees depending on your latitude and the season, so use it only as a tie-breaker alongside a stronger method, never as your primary bearing.

sections.heading: Dead Reckoning: Course, Pace Count, and Aiming Off
sections.body:
Every method so far tells you which way is north. Dead reckoning is what you do with that bearing once the fog rolls in and you can no longer see the landmark you were walking toward — it turns a single compass heading into a full navigational plan by adding the one ingredient direction alone can't give you: distance.

Start with the correction every dead-reckoning plan depends on and every beginner forgets: your compass needle points at magnetic north, not true north, and a map's grid lines point at true north, so the two disagree by an amount called magnetic declination that changes with your location and drifts slowly over years. Your map's margin carries a declination diagram for its year of survey; a current online or app value is safer for anything printed more than a few years ago. The conversion follows a fixed rule regardless of direction of travel: to turn a true bearing taken off a map into the magnetic bearing you'll dial into your compass, subtract an easterly declination or add a westerly one (the old surveyor's mnemonic is 'east is least, west is best'). Picture a hillwalker on a moor in thick mist, having plotted a true bearing of 130° off the map to reach a saddle between two summits, in a region where the declination is 3° west: dial the compass to 130° + 3° = 133° magnetic, and that — not 130° — is the heading to walk.

Distance comes from your feet. Calibrate a personal pace count once, on flat ground, over a known 100 m — a running-track straight or an odometer-measured stretch of quiet road both work — by counting every time the same foot strikes the ground and averaging three walk-throughs; a typical adult lands somewhere around 60-70 paces per 100 m, but the only count that matters is your own, and it lengthens noticeably (add roughly 10% or more) on steep uphill, in soft sand, or wading through deep snow. A knotted cord or a set of ranger beads, slid down one at a time every hundred paces, keeps the tally honest over distances long enough that your head would otherwise lose count.

The single technique that turns this from a neat trick into a genuinely trustworthy field skill is aiming off. If your target is a cabin on a river you won't see until you're on top of it, don't aim your bearing directly at the cabin — deliberately offset it 5-10° to one side, say upstream. Walk your corrected bearing and pace count, and you will hit the river with total certainty; because you know which side you biased toward, you know without any doubt or backtracking that the cabin lies downstream of wherever you struck the water. Search-and-rescue teams and orienteers use exactly this trick to move confidently through zero-visibility forest, fog, or whiteout, because it converts an aim that could be wrong by a few degrees into a plan that cannot fail — you will always know which way to turn.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: None of this requires anything exotic — most of it fits in a jacket pocket, and you can assemble the whole kit from an outdoor-recreation store, a general hardware store, and a drawer at home.
ingredients: A baseplate orienteering compass (a $10-25 model with a rotating degree-marked bezel and a clear, flat base for map work) — skip a bezel-less keychain compass, it can't take an accurate bearing

A current topographic map of your practice area with its printed declination diagram intact, from an outdoor-recreation store, a park visitor center, or printed at home from a national mapping agency's site
A smartphone or handheld GPS unit, used only AFTER each drill to check your work rather than as the primary tool, or the skill never builds
An analog wristwatch with hands, or a plain paper clock face drawn on cardboard with pencil hands, for the watch-and-sun method
A straight stick about a meter long, plus two small pebbles or twigs to mark shadow positions, for the shadow-stick method
A pair of polarized sunglasses or a small polarizing camera filter, from an optics/photography retailer or any general store's sunglasses rack, for reading polarized skylight under overcast
A notebook and pencil, kept in a sealed sandwich bag against rain, for logging bearings, pace counts, and declination readings
A knotted length of cord (a knot tied every 100 paces) or a set of pace-counting beads, from an outdoor or military-surplus store, for tracking dead-reckoning distance
Optional: a simple planisphere or star wheel, from a hobby/telescope shop or printed from an astronomy-education site, for practicing the star methods on a clear night

sections.heading: A Weekend Drill: Calibrate Yourself Against a Known Bearing
sections.body: The only way any of this becomes reliable under real pressure is to test it against ground truth you already know, in good weather, before you ever need it in bad. This drill takes under two hours and needs nothing but a park or schoolyard, a straight stick, and a compass.
steps: Find a running track, football pitch, or any straight, flat stretch you can measure — a standard track straightaway is 100 m, or measure 100 m yourself with a long tape measure or a car's odometer along a quiet road (watch for traffic if you use one).

Walk the 100 m at your normal outdoor pace, counting a 'pace' every time the same foot (say, your left) touches the ground. Repeat it three times and average the three counts — that number is your personal pace-count-per-100 m, and it's the only one that matters; published averages (often quoted around 65) are just a starting expectation.

Around local solar noon, push a straight stick about a meter long vertically into flat open ground and mark the very tip of its shortest shadow with a pebble. That pebble marks true north from the stick's base in the Northern Hemisphere (true south in the Southern Hemisphere) — this is your ground truth for the whole drill.

Lay your baseplate compass flat, sight from the stick's base to the pebble, and read the magnetic bearing. The difference between that reading and true north/south is your local magnetic declination right now, at this exact spot — compare it to your map's declination diagram or a current online value; if it's off by more than 2-3°, check for nearby metal (a belt buckle, a chain-link fence, a parked car) and repeat somewhere clear of it.

Pick a real landmark at least 500 m away — a water tower, a church steeple, a radio mast — take its magnetic bearing, correct it to a true bearing using the declination you just measured, and plot the line on your map. If the line runs believably close to the landmark's actual mapped position, your whole chain of skills — shadow, compass, declination, and map plotting — just checked out against itself.

Finish by walking 200 m on a magnetic bearing of your own choosing, using only your compass and pace count, with no path or landmark to follow — and deliberately aim off 5-10° to one side of some line feature you know crosses your route (a fence, a trail, a tree line), so that when you reach it you know with certainty which way to turn. This exercise — bearing, pace count, aiming off — is the actual skill search-and-rescue teams and competitive orienteers rely on to move with total confidence through fog, dense forest, or whiteout, and it's worth more than memorizing any star chart on its own.

guides.title: Topographic Maps & Terrain Reading
guides.summary: A practical guide to reading a topographic map itself: how contour lines encode elevation and reveal landform shape, how map scale and coordinate systems translate paper distances into real ground positions, and how to orient a map, correct for declination, and plan a route using nothing but the sheet in your hands.

sections.heading: What Contour Lines Represent
sections.body: A contour line traces every point on the map that sits at exactly the same elevation above a reference datum, usually mean sea level. Walk along a single contour line in the real world and, in principle, you neither climb nor descend — you stay level, the way a shoreline traces around a hill at a fixed height. The vertical distance between adjacent contour lines is the contour interval, printed in the map's margin (commonly 40 feet on USGS 1:24,000 quadrangles, 10 or 20 meters on many international sheets, sometimes as fine as 5 feet on flat coastal terrain or as coarse as 100 feet in steep mountain country). Every fourth or fifth contour is drawn heavier and usually labeled with its elevation — this is an index contour — so you can count intervals between labeled lines rather than tracing every faint line back to a known point. On a map with a 40-foot interval and index contours every fifth line, the index contours might read 2,000, 2,200, and 2,400 feet, with three unlabeled contours between them at 2,040, 2,080, and 2,120 feet. Closely spaced lines mean elevation changes rapidly over a short horizontal distance — steep ground; widely spaced lines mean the ground is nearly flat.

sections.heading: Reading Contour Patterns: Ridges vs. Valleys
sections.body: Contour lines describe landforms through their shape, and two patterns account for most terrain you will navigate: ridges and valleys. A ridge is a long, elevated spine of land, and its contour lines bulge outward, away from the high ground, as they cross it — each contour makes a rounded or pointed protrusion pointing downhill, away from the summit. A valley or drainage is the mirror image: contour lines bend inward, forming a V or U shape that points toward higher ground, upstream, toward the head of the drainage. This is the single most useful rule in topographic reading: on a stream or valley, the contour's point always aims uphill, in the direction the water is flowing from, not toward. If you are standing in unfamiliar terrain and can see a drainage's V-shaped notch pointing north on the map, the water in that drainage is flowing south, downhill, away from the point. Confusing this rule — assuming a V points downstream — is one of the most common and consequential map-reading errors, since it can lead you to follow a drainage the wrong direction or misjudge which side of a ridge you are standing on. Practice by finding a known stream on a map and confirming its contours point upstream at every bend; the pattern becomes intuitive after a few examples.

sections.heading: Saddles, Depressions, and Other Landforms
sections.body: Beyond ridges and valleys, a handful of other contour patterns recur often enough to memorize on sight. A saddle, or col, is a low point between two higher points — the dip in a ridgeline where a trail commonly crosses — and it appears on the map as an hourglass or bowtie shape, two sets of contours pinching toward each other from opposite sides between two peaks. A summit or knob shows as a set of concentric closed loops shrinking toward a single point, typically labeled with a spot elevation and an X or triangle. A depression — a sinkhole, quarry, or closed basin with no outlet — looks like a summit's closed loops but is marked with short perpendicular tick marks, called hachures, pointing inward toward the low point; without those hachures there is no way to tell a hole in the ground from a hill, since both are just closed circles. Cliffs and very steep faces show as contour lines merging together or even touching, sometimes replaced by a distinct cliff symbol — a serrated or hachured line — where the slope is too steep to draw individual contours legibly. Recognizing these shapes at a glance, rather than mentally converting each line to a number, is what lets an experienced map reader see the terrain in three dimensions from a flat sheet of paper.

sections.heading: Map Scale and Representative Fractions
sections.body: Every topographic map states its scale as a representative fraction, a ratio comparing one unit of distance on the map to the same unit on the ground. A USGS 7.5-minute quadrangle is printed at 1:24,000, meaning one inch on the paper equals 24,000 inches, or exactly 2,000 feet, on the ground; one centimeter equals 240 meters. Smaller-scale maps cover more area with less detail — a 1:100,000 map shows roughly 1 inch to 1.6 miles, useful for regional planning but too coarse to spot a small cliff band — while larger-scale maps like 1:12,000 or 1:10,000 show fine detail over a small area, valuable for technical terrain but requiring many sheets to cover a trip. Most topo maps also print a graphic scale bar in the margin, a ruled line marked in miles, feet, or kilometers, which is more reliable than the printed ratio if the map has been photocopied or resized, since a graphic bar shrinks or grows along with the map while the fraction does not. To measure a winding trail's real distance, lay a piece of string or the edge of a strip of paper along each segment, mark the cumulative length, then compare it against the scale bar. A quick sanity check: on a 1:24,000 map, a straight-line inch is very close to one third of a mile.

sections.heading: True North, Grid North, and Magnetic North
sections.body: A topographic map deals with three different norths, and confusing them is the most common cause of a compass bearing that leads you astray. True north is the direction along the earth's surface toward the geographic North Pole, the axis the planet spins on; it is the north that meridians of longitude converge toward, and it is what a topo map's edges are normally aligned to. Grid north is the direction of the vertical lines of the map's UTM or state-plane grid overlay; because a flat grid cannot perfectly match a curved earth, grid north differs from true north by a small amount called grid convergence, usually under a degree or two on a single quadrangle and often ignored for foot travel. Magnetic north is the direction a compass needle actually points, toward the wandering magnetic north pole in the Canadian Arctic, and it differs from true north by an amount called declination that varies by location and slowly changes from year to year. In parts of the western United States declination runs roughly 12 to 15 degrees east; in parts of the northeast it can be several degrees west. The map's margin states the declination for that specific quadrangle and the year it was surveyed, alongside a small diagram showing all three norths as diverging arrows.

sections.heading: Understanding and Applying Declination
sections.body: Declination is the angular difference, in degrees, between magnetic north (where your compass needle points) and true north (the direction the map's grid is normally drawn to). If a map's declination diagram shows 14 degrees east, magnetic north lies 14 degrees to the east of true north at that location. This matters because every bearing you read off the map is a true bearing, but every bearing you follow with an uncorrected compass is a magnetic bearing — mixing the two without adjusting will put you off course by exactly the declination angle, which over a mile of travel can mean drifting a quarter mile or more from your intended point. To convert a true bearing, read from the map, into a magnetic bearing to follow with the compass, subtract the declination where it is easterly and add it where it is westerly. The common memory aid is 'east is least, west is best' — subtract for east, add for west — when going from true to magnetic. Many modern baseplate compasses have an adjustable declination screw that lets you dial in the local value once, so every bearing you read off the housing is already corrected and the arithmetic disappears entirely. Because magnetic north drifts over time, always check the survey year printed on the declination diagram and, for older maps, look up the current value rather than trusting a decades-old figure.

sections.heading: Orienting the Map to the Terrain
sections.body: Orienting a map means rotating it so the features drawn on paper line up with the same features in the real landscape, north on the map pointing toward actual north, which makes every landform on the sheet visually match what you are looking at. The simplest method uses a compass: lay the compass flat on the map with its edge along one of the map's north-south grid lines, rotate the housing to the declination-corrected reading for north, then turn the map and compass together as a single unit until the magnetic needle sits inside the housing's orienting arrow. The map is now oriented to true north regardless of which direction you happen to be facing. A rougher but often faster method uses terrain association: turn the map until a prominent visible feature, such as a distinctive peak, lake, or river bend, points from your estimated position on the map toward that same feature in front of you; if two or three features line up at once, the map is oriented closely enough for route-finding. Orienting the map is worth doing every time you stop to navigate, because a map read while pointed the wrong way forces you to mentally mirror-flip left and right, a common source of navigation mistakes at trail junctions and stream crossings.

sections.heading: The UTM Grid System
sections.body: The Universal Transverse Mercator, or UTM, system divides the earth into 60 numbered zones, each 6 degrees of longitude wide, and within each zone lays a simple grid of squares measured in meters rather than degrees, making it far easier to use on foot than latitude and longitude. A UTM coordinate has three parts: the zone number and letter, such as 12S, identifying a 6-degree-wide band; an easting, the distance in meters east of a reference line within the zone, typically a six-digit number; and a northing, the distance in meters north of the equator, typically a seven-digit number north of the equator. A coordinate such as 12S 456700mE 4432900mN pins a location to within one meter if every digit is used, or within 100 meters if only the leading digits before the final three of each number are read — the common field practice of reading a grid reference to the nearest 100 meters. Topo maps print thin blue or black UTM grid lines at a fixed spacing, commonly every 1,000 meters at 1:24,000 scale, with the full easting and northing values labeled at intervals along the margin. Because the grid squares are true meters on the ground rather than a projected distortion, UTM makes measuring real distances and plotting a GPS position simple arithmetic rather than trigonometry.

sections.heading: Latitude and Longitude on a Topo Map
sections.body: Latitude and longitude describe a position on the globe as two angles: latitude is the angle north or south of the equator, running from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 at the poles, and longitude is the angle east or west of the Prime Meridian running through Greenwich, England, from 0 to 180 degrees in each direction. A topo map's outer border is marked in latitude and longitude, usually as degrees, minutes, and seconds — a USGS 7.5-minute quadrangle covers exactly 7.5 minutes of latitude by 7.5 minutes of longitude, one minute being one-sixtieth of a degree — with tick marks along the edges at regular intervals, such as every 2 minutes 30 seconds. Because one degree of longitude covers less real ground the farther you are from the equator, while one degree of latitude is a nearly constant distance everywhere, about 69 miles or 111 kilometers, latitude and longitude are less convenient than UTM for measuring distance by hand, though they remain the universal system for referencing a location on any device or in any country. Coordinates are often given in decimal degrees today, such as 44.2619, -71.3033, rather than degrees-minutes-seconds; either format converts directly, and most GPS units and mapping apps let you switch the display to match whatever the map or the person you are coordinating with is using.

sections.heading: Map Symbols and Legend Conventions
sections.body: Topographic maps compress an enormous amount of information into a standardized set of symbols, and reading them fluently is as much a part of map literacy as understanding contour lines. Color carries meaning first: black is generally used for man-made features such as roads, buildings, and most labels; blue for water, including streams, lakes, wetlands, and glaciers; green for vegetation cover, where dense green usually means forest or heavy brush and white or tan means open ground; brown for contour lines and other terrain features; and red for major highways or, on some series, public land survey lines. Line style distinguishes feature types within a color: a solid black line is typically a paved road, a pair of dashed lines an unpaved or four-wheel-drive road, a single dashed line a trail, and a row of dots a boundary such as a park or wilderness line. Point symbols mark specific features — a small black square for a building, a cross for a church, a crossed pick and shovel for a mine, a tent icon for a campground. The map's marginal legend explains any symbols specific to that particular series, but the core conventions of blue water, green vegetation, and brown terrain are consistent enough across most national mapping agencies that recognizing them becomes automatic with practice, letting you read a map's story at a glance rather than symbol by symbol.

sections.heading: Estimating Slope and Gradient from Contour Spacing
sections.body: The horizontal distance between adjacent contour lines is a direct, measurable readout of slope steepness, and learning to judge it at a glance is one of the most practical topo-map skills for route planning. Gradient is simply rise over run: if two contour lines 40 feet apart in elevation are separated by 200 feet of horizontal map distance, the slope is 40 divided by 200, or 20 percent, roughly 11 degrees, a moderate hillside. The same 40-foot interval compressed into just 40 feet of horizontal distance yields a 100 percent grade, a 45-degree slope, steep enough to require careful footing or scrambling. As lines get closer together the slope angle rises faster than the percentage alone suggests, because percent grade and degrees are not linearly related — a 100 percent grade is 45 degrees, but a 200 percent grade is about 63 degrees, not 90. A useful field habit is to measure, with a ruler or the edge of a compass baseplate, how many contour lines cross a fixed distance, say a quarter inch on a 1:24,000 map, which is 500 feet on the ground, along your intended route; six or more index-interval crossings in that span usually signals slope steep enough to reconsider, especially with a pack, snow, or loose rock underfoot. Working through a few examples by hand builds the intuition to judge slope by eye on any map without recalculating each time.

sections.heading: Building a Topo Map Field Kit
sections.body: A dependable topo-map kit is inexpensive and small enough to fit in a jacket pocket, but each piece serves a distinct purpose that is hard to substitute in the field. The map itself is the base layer of information, whether that is a paper sheet in a waterproof case or a downloaded offline layer in a mapping app with the phone kept in airplane mode to save battery. A baseplate compass with a rotating bezel and adjustable declination lets you take and follow bearings directly off the map's edge. A pencil, not a pen, marks waypoints, timestamps, and route lines directly on the paper, since bearings and notes often need correcting. A protractor or a compass's built-in scale reads bearings and angles precisely. A romer, a small L-shaped ruler printed with a scale matching the map and often built into the compass baseplate, lets you plot or read UTM coordinates to the nearest 100 meters without doing arithmetic. A small notebook turns single data points into a record you can reconstruct later. None of these items alone replaces sound judgment, but together they remove the guesswork from the two questions that matter most in the field: where am I, and which direction do I need to go.
ingredients: Topographic map (waterproofed paper, or an offline digital layer)
Baseplate compass with adjustable declination
Pencil
Protractor or romer (UTM plotting scale)
Small notebook
Ruler or string for measuring distance along a route
Spare batteries (if relying on a phone, GPS, or headlamp)

sections.heading: How to Take a Compass Bearing From a Map and Follow It
sections.body: Taking a bearing from the map and walking it in the field is the core mechanical skill that ties together scale, north references, declination, and orientation into a single repeatable procedure. Practice it first on a short, easily verified route, such as a straight trail segment with a landmark at each end, before relying on it in terrain where a wrong turn matters. The procedure below produces a magnetic bearing, ready to follow with an uncorrected compass, by building the declination adjustment in as its own discrete step rather than trying to do the arithmetic under pressure.
steps: Identify your current position and your destination on the map, and mark each lightly with a pencil dot.
Lay the compass baseplate flat on the map so its straight edge connects the two points, with the direction-of-travel arrow pointing from your position toward the destination.

Without moving the baseplate, rotate the compass housing until its orienting lines and orienting arrow align with the map's north-south grid lines, with the orienting arrow pointing to true north on the map.
Read the true bearing where the index line meets the housing's degree scale.

Adjust for declination: subtract the local value for easterly declination, or add it for westerly declination, to convert the true bearing into a magnetic bearing (skip this step if your compass has a preset declination adjustment).
Hold the compass flat and level in front of you, then rotate your entire body until the magnetic needle settles inside the outlined orienting arrow, commonly taught as 'putting red in the shed.'
Sight along the direction-of-travel arrow to a visible landmark ahead, such as a distinctive tree, rock, or terrain feature, and walk to it.

Repeat the sighting-and-walking process landmark by landmark, checking the compass periodically to confirm you are still tracking the bearing, until you reach the destination or a recognizable feature confirms your position.

sections.heading: Planning a Route: Identifying Passable Terrain and Hazards
sections.body: Reading a topo map to plan a route is the practical synthesis of every skill above: scale tells you how far, contour spacing tells you how steep, and landform patterns tell you what kind of ground you will cross. Start by marking your start and end points, then look for a corridor between them where contour lines stay relatively far apart along the whole way, since wide spacing usually means a walkable grade while any stretch where the lines bunch tightly or merge into a solid brown mass signals a cliff or a slope too steep for casual travel. Ridgelines often make efficient, well-drained travel corridors with good visibility, while valley bottoms may hold water, dense brush, or loose rock but offer a gentler, more predictable grade; a route that sidehills across a slope, crossing contour lines at a shallow angle rather than straight up or down, can also cut elevation gain at the cost of extra distance. Watch specifically for danger signs: contour lines converging into an unbroken dark band, a tight cluster of closed loops beside a valley that can mark a rockslide or avalanche path, or a drainage crossing your route that will run as a real stream after rain even if it looks minor on paper. Cross-check any doubtful stretch against satellite imagery or a recent trip report where available, since a map surveyed decades ago will not show a washed-out trail or a fallen bridge, and always keep a backup route in mind in case the primary one proves impassable.

guides.safetyNote: Contour lines that converge into a solid band or merge together indicate cliffs or extremely steep terrain. Never assume a route is passable on foot just because it looks short on the map — confirm with visible ground truth, carry a backup route, and set a turn-around time before committing to any stretch where contours are tightly packed.

guides.title: Modern GPS, GNSS & Digital Navigation
guides.summary: GPS is a triumph of applied physics disguised as a convenience feature: a constellation of atomic clocks in orbit lets a handheld receiver compute its position to within a few meters anywhere on Earth. This guide explains how satellite positioning actually works, why it sometimes fails, and how to use it as a powerful tool without becoming helpless without it.

sections.heading: What GPS Actually Measures: Trilateration Explained
sections.body: A GPS satellite does not know where you are. Instead, it continuously broadcasts a radio signal encoding its own precise orbital position and the exact time the signal was transmitted. Your receiver notes the moment the signal arrives and subtracts the transmit time to get a time-of-flight, which it multiplies by the speed of light (about 299,792,458 meters per second) to get a distance, called a pseudorange. That single measurement only tells you that you are somewhere on the surface of a sphere centered on that satellite, with the pseudorange as the radius. A second satellite gives you a second sphere; where the two spheres intersect is a circle. A third satellite's sphere intersects that circle at essentially two points, one of which is usually absurd (thousands of kilometers off Earth's surface or deep underground) and can be discarded. This process of pinpointing a location by measuring distances from multiple known reference points is called trilateration, and it is the mathematical core of every satellite navigation system in use today, from a hiking GPS to an airliner's flight management computer.

sections.heading: Why You Need Four Satellites, Not Three
sections.body: In principle, three distance measurements are enough to solve for three unknowns: your latitude, longitude, and altitude. In practice, GPS receivers always need a signal from a fourth satellite, and the reason comes down to clocks. The satellites carry atomic clocks accurate to a few billionths of a second, but putting an atomic clock in a $150 handheld receiver is not practical, so consumer receivers use a cheap quartz crystal oscillator that drifts by a small but significant amount. That drift, called the receiver clock bias, is an unknown fourth variable in the position equations. A fourth satellite measurement supplies the extra equation needed to solve for all four unknowns simultaneously: x, y, z, and the receiver's own clock error. The receiver software effectively synchronizes its clock to the satellite constellation on every fix, which is why a even a cheap GPS chip can keep sub-microsecond time. With only three satellites in view, a receiver can sometimes still produce a rough 2D fix by assuming a known altitude, but a full three-dimensional position requires four or more satellites above the horizon simultaneously.

sections.heading: Atomic Clocks and the Relativity Correction
sections.body: GPS is one of the few pieces of consumer technology where the engineering breaks without accounting for both special and general relativity. Because light travels roughly 30 centimeters per nanosecond, a timing error of just one microsecond translates into a position error of about 300 meters, so the satellite clocks must be extraordinarily precise, hence the cesium and rubidium atomic clocks aboard each one. Einstein's special relativity says a clock moving fast relative to an observer ticks slower; GPS satellites orbit at roughly 14,000 kilometers per hour, which causes their onboard clocks to run about 7 microseconds per day slower than clocks on the ground. General relativity says a clock in a weaker gravitational field ticks faster; at the GPS orbital altitude of about 20,200 kilometers, Earth's gravity is much weaker than at the surface, causing the satellite clocks to run about 45 microseconds per day faster. The two effects do not cancel out, leaving a net gain of roughly 38 microseconds per day. Engineers correct for this before launch by deliberately tuning each satellite's clock frequency slightly slower than the standard cesium frequency, so that once in orbit it ticks at the correct rate. Without this correction, GPS position errors would accumulate by about 10 kilometers per day.

sections.heading: The Four GNSS Constellations: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou
sections.body: GPS, operated by the United States Space Force, was the first fully operational global system, reaching full capability in 1995 with a baseline of 24 satellites in six orbital planes about 20,200 kilometers up. It is no longer the only game in the sky. Russia's GLONASS reached full global coverage in the 1990s and again after a 2011 restoration, using 24 satellites at a slightly lower altitude of about 19,100 kilometers. The European Union's Galileo, declared operational in 2016, was designed from the start under civilian rather than military control and offers a high-accuracy open signal along with an encrypted commercial service. China's BeiDou completed its third-generation global constellation in 2020, mixing satellites in medium orbit with some in geostationary and inclined geosynchronous orbits over the Asia-Pacific region for extra regional coverage. Collectively these four systems, plus regional augmentation systems like Japan's QZSS and India's NavIC, are referred to as GNSS, or Global Navigation Satellite Systems. Nearly every modern smartphone and dedicated GPS receiver tracks satellites from several of these constellations at once, which is why phones today typically lock onto 20 to 30 satellites rather than the 6 to 10 available from GPS alone, improving both fix speed and accuracy.

sections.heading: Dilution of Precision: Why Accuracy Varies
sections.body: Two fixes made with the same number of satellites and the same receiver can differ in accuracy by an order of magnitude, and the reason is geometry, not signal quality. Dilution of precision, or DOP, describes how the spatial arrangement of the satellites you are using amplifies or suppresses the underlying ranging error. If your visible satellites are spread widely across the sky in different directions, their spheres intersect at a sharp, well-defined point, and DOP is low, meaning good accuracy. If the satellites are clustered together in one part of the sky, for instance all low near the horizon on one side, the spheres intersect at a shallow, elongated angle, and small ranging errors translate into large position errors; DOP is high. Receivers report several flavors of this number: HDOP for horizontal accuracy, VDOP for vertical, and PDOP or GDOP for combined position or position-plus-time. A PDOP under 4 is generally considered excellent, while values above 8 indicate an unreliable fix even if the receiver shows several bars of signal. This is also why altitude readings from GPS are typically much less accurate than horizontal position: satellites are never visible below the horizon, so the geometry for solving vertical position is inherently weaker than for solving horizontal position.

sections.heading: Urban Canyons and Multipath Interference
sections.body: Walk down a street lined with tall buildings and watch a phone's map jump your blue dot across the street, into a building, or several hundred meters down the block, and you are watching two related problems at once. The first is simple blockage: buildings physically hide large portions of the sky, cutting the number of visible satellites and often leaving a poor, high-DOP geometry skewed toward whatever narrow strip of sky remains open overhead. The second, more insidious problem is multipath interference. A GPS signal can reflect off a glass facade or a metal surface before reaching the receiver, arriving slightly later than the direct signal would have, or arriving only as a reflection with no direct path available at all. Because the receiver calculates distance from signal travel time, that extra bounce reads as extra distance, and the resulting pseudorange is simply wrong. In a dense urban canyon, multipath errors from reflected signals routinely account for position errors of tens of meters, far larger than the few meters typical in open sky. Surveying-grade receivers use specialized antenna designs and signal-processing techniques to reject multipath, but consumer devices generally cannot, which is why dropped pins in cities should always be treated with some skepticism.

sections.heading: Canopy, Indoors, and Weak-Signal Environments
sections.body: GPS signals are remarkably weak by the time they reach the ground: a satellite transmits with roughly the power of a household light bulb, spread across a beam covering nearly half the planet from 20,200 kilometers away, so the signal arriving at your receiver is buried well below the noise floor and only recoverable through sophisticated correlation techniques. That faintness makes GPS vulnerable to attenuation. Dense forest canopy, especially when wet, absorbs and scatters the roughly 1.5 gigahertz L-band signal significantly, since water is an efficient absorber at that frequency; under a thick, rain-soaked canopy a receiver may lose lock entirely or hold only a degraded fix with poor accuracy. Indoors, walls and roofing materials attenuate the signal far more severely, and most consumer receivers cannot acquire a usable fix inside a typical building at all, though some high-sensitivity chips can hold a weak, already-acquired fix for a short time near windows. Canyons, caves, and dense urban interiors present the same problem in different forms. The practical lesson is that GPS reliability is not binary; it degrades gradually with obstruction, and a receiver reporting a fix under heavy canopy or near a building should be trusted less than the same device reporting a fix under open sky.

sections.heading: Jamming and Spoofing: When GPS Lies to You
sections.body: Jamming and spoofing are distinct threats, and understanding the difference matters. Jamming is brute-force denial: a device broadcasts noise or a strong signal on the same frequency GPS uses, overwhelming the real satellite signals so the receiver simply cannot lock on and either shows no fix or reports the last known position. Cheap, illegal jammers, often marketed to defeat vehicle tracking, can disrupt GPS reception for hundreds of meters around them and have occasionally caused documented problems near airports and ports. Spoofing is more dangerous because it is deceptive rather than merely disruptive: an attacker broadcasts counterfeit signals that mimic real GPS satellites but carry false timing or position data, tricking the receiver into computing a fix that is confidently wrong rather than simply absent. Documented spoofing incidents include ships in the Black Sea and eastern Mediterranean showing false positions many kilometers from their true location, and aircraft navigation systems in active conflict zones reporting impossible jumps or the wrong airport entirely. Because a spoofed receiver reports high confidence and normal-looking coordinates, spoofing is far harder to detect than an outright signal loss, which is precisely why autonomous vehicles, shipping, and aviation increasingly cross-check GPS against inertial sensors and other independent references rather than trusting it alone.

sections.heading: How Your Phone Gets a Fix So Fast: Assisted GPS
sections.body: A GPS receiver starting completely cold, with no prior knowledge of its location, time, or which satellites are overhead, must download a slow navigation message broadcast at only 50 bits per second, a process that can take 30 seconds to several minutes before it computes its first fix. Smartphones almost never make you wait that long, because they use Assisted GPS, or A-GPS. When your phone has a cellular or WiFi data connection, it downloads the current satellite almanac and precise ephemeris data, along with a rough estimate of your location derived from nearby cell towers or known WiFi access point locations, over the fast internet connection instead of the slow satellite broadcast. Armed with that head start, the GPS chip knows roughly where it is and which satellites should be visible, so it can lock onto weak signals and compute a fix in just a few seconds rather than minutes, a dramatic improvement known as reducing time-to-first-fix. This is also why phones can still show an approximate location with GPS switched off or unavailable, since cell-tower and WiFi-based positioning alone can locate a device to within tens to a few hundred meters using databases of known signal locations, a useful fallback though far less precise than a true satellite fix.

sections.heading: Waypoints, Tracks, and Routes: The Units of Digital Navigation
sections.body: Every digital navigation device, from a dedicated handheld GPS to a smartphone hiking app, organizes information around three basic building blocks. A waypoint is a single saved coordinate marking a specific point of interest, such as your parked car, a water source, a campsite, or a trailhead; it is the digital equivalent of circling a spot on a paper map. A track, sometimes called a track log or breadcrumb trail, is an automatically recorded series of coordinates the device logs at regular intervals as you move, building a continuous record of exactly where you have been; tracks are invaluable for retracing your steps or later analyzing a route's distance and elevation profile. A route is different from a track in that it is planned rather than recorded: it is an ordered sequence of waypoints you intend to travel between, often with the device calculating bearing and distance from one to the next, or in road navigation, calculating a suggested path of travel along known roads. Understanding this distinction matters practically, since a device typically has separate menus and separate storage limits for waypoints, tracks, and routes, and confusing them, for instance trying to navigate to a track rather than a waypoint, is a common source of user frustration in the field.

sections.heading: Datums and WGS84: Why Coordinate Systems Must Match
sections.body: Earth is not a perfect sphere; it bulges slightly at the equator and has a lumpy, irregular gravitational field, so any coordinate system needs a mathematical reference model, called a datum, that approximates Earth's shape and defines an origin point for measuring latitude and longitude against it. The datum used almost universally by modern GPS devices, mapping apps, and GNSS systems is WGS84, short for World Geodetic System 1984, a global ellipsoid model maintained and periodically refined by the United States government specifically to support satellite navigation. Older paper maps, particularly topographic maps printed before the 1990s, were often drawn using regional datums optimized for local accuracy, such as NAD27 in North America or various national datums elsewhere, and these older datums can disagree with WGS84 by anywhere from a few meters to several hundred meters depending on the region. The practical danger is that coordinates are just numbers; a latitude and longitude pair read off a device set to one datum and plotted on a map or entered into a device using a different datum will point to a real but wrong location on the ground, with no warning that anything is amiss. Always confirm that your GPS device's datum setting matches the datum printed on any paper map you are cross-referencing, and default to WGS84 whenever there is doubt, since it is what virtually all current digital maps and satellite systems assume.

sections.heading: Building a Digital Navigation Field Kit
sections.body: Reliable digital navigation in the field depends on more than a single device, since batteries die, screens crack, and signal is never guaranteed. A well-thought-out kit treats the electronics as one redundant layer among several rather than the sole plan.
ingredients: A GPS-capable smartphone or dedicated handheld GPS unit with offline map tiles for your area downloaded in advance
A portable battery pack or power bank, fully charged, with the correct charging cable
The device set to airplane mode or GPS-only mode in the field to conserve battery, since cellular searching drains power fast with no signal
A physical paper topographic map of the area, printed or waterproofed, using the same datum as your GPS device
A baseplate compass and the working knowledge to use it with the map
A written or printed list of key waypoint coordinates (trailhead, campsite, water sources, bailout points) as a backup in case the device is lost or fails
Spare batteries if your device uses replaceable batteries rather than a sealed rechargeable cell
A small notebook and pencil to log position and time manually at intervals, as a low-tech track log

sections.heading: How to Mark and Navigate Back to a Waypoint
sections.body: One of the most immediately useful GPS skills is marking your current position so you can find your way back to it later, whether that is a parked vehicle, a water cache, or a campsite. The general procedure below applies, with minor menu differences, to virtually every dedicated handheld GPS and most smartphone hiking apps.
steps: Stand still at the exact location you want to save and let the device settle onto a stable fix, ideally with a low DOP reading and several satellites locked, before proceeding.
Open the device's Mark Waypoint function, usually a dedicated button on handheld units or a menu option labeled 'Save Location' or 'Drop Pin' on phone apps.
Give the waypoint a short, memorable name or number, such as 'CAR' or 'CAMP1', rather than accepting an anonymous default label, since you may save many waypoints over a trip.
Confirm the save and verify the waypoint now appears in the device's waypoint list with reasonable coordinates.
When you are ready to return, open the waypoint list, select the saved point, and choose the 'Go To' or 'Navigate' function.
Follow the on-screen bearing and distance readout, which continuously updates as you move, keeping the directional arrow or compass needle pointed straight ahead.

Periodically cross-check the device's suggested direction against visible terrain features and, if carrying one, a physical compass bearing, rather than following the screen blindly through terrain you can see is wrong.

Upon arrival, the distance readout will approach zero; stop and visually confirm you have reached the intended feature, since GPS accuracy of a few meters can still place you slightly off from a small target.

sections.heading: GPS as a Tool, Not a Replacement for Map and Compass
sections.body: Every advantage described in this guide comes with an honest caveat: GPS is a battery-powered electronic device, and every battery-powered electronic device eventually fails, whether from a dead battery, a cracked screen, water damage, cold weather sapping charge faster than expected, or simply being dropped down a slope. A GPS receiver can also lose signal for reasons entirely outside your control, from dense canopy to a canyon to a satellite constellation temporarily poorly positioned overhead. None of this makes GPS unreliable in the way that matters most: as a primary tool for precise position-finding, elevation tracking, and retracing a route, it is dramatically more accurate and far less effortful than traditional methods. The mistake is treating it as infallible rather than as one input among several. Experienced navigators use GPS the way a pilot uses an autopilot: actively, gratefully, and never blindly. Carry a physical map and compass as backup, know how to use them before you need them, periodically note your position by traditional means even while primarily navigating digitally, and treat any GPS reading that disagrees sharply with visible terrain as a prompt to double-check rather than a command to follow. Redundancy, not brand-new technology, is what actually keeps people found.

guides.safetyNote: GPS devices can fail, lose signal, or be spoofed by false signals — always carry a physical map and compass as backup and know how to navigate with them before you need to rely on that skill.
